title: A Sikh prime minister
hookLine: a soft-spoken Sikh economist leads India as prime minister

lines: A PALE BLUE TURBAN ON TELEVISION.
cards: On a television screen, a man in a pale blue turban reads a speech. He doesn't shout or wave his arms. His voice is so soft that people lean toward the set to hear him.

He's an economist, a man of reports, tables and budgets, and he has just become prime minister of India. His given name is Manmohan, and he carries the name Singh, as Sikh men do. The country comes to know him as Dr.
Singh. Today: a Sikh prime minister.

teach.h: A LIST OF DESKS, NOT SPEECHES.
teach.b: First, the road there. Dr. Singh didn't come up through rallies.

He was a scholar of economics who worked in government offices for years, and served as finance minister before he led the country. His public biography reads like a list of desks, not a list of speeches.

teach.h: A TURBAN AT THE HEAD OF GOVERNMENT.
teach.b: Second, what people saw: a turbaned Sikh at the head of India's government, wearing his faith openly, in the same country this path has followed through some of its hardest years.
Some Sikhs, and others, spoke of it as a moment worth noticing. Third, the manner. He was known for a quiet, careful style, and for listening more than he spoke.
People argued about his policies, as they argue about every leader's, and this lesson takes no side on them. The thing to notice is the tone.
At Ang 470 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that sweetness and humility are the essence of all virtues. Not loudness, not winning the room. Fourth, the everyday version.
Most quiet service never reaches a television: a clerk who checks your form twice so it won't be rejected, a nurse on a night shift, a city planner you only notice when the bus comes on time.
Sikhs speak of seva as service that doesn't ask to be seen, and it can happen at a desk as well as in a langar hall.

how: Sikhs serve in public office in India and elsewhere while keeping the turban and the articles of faith; in the tradition, service done well and without seeking credit is counted as seva.

o: shyness that keeps someone out of public life
humility, a gentle and quiet way of serving
politeness shown only to people above you

games.q: the prime minister and the line — tap the pairs.
p: an economist who led India's government
work that doesn't ask to be seen

s: he rose to office mainly through loud rallies
he came up as an economist in government offices and served as finance minister.
he led India's government wearing his turban
he wore his faith openly as prime minister.
people argued about them, as with every leader; the lesson only notices his manner.

games.q: you're a soft-spoken expert, and you're asked to lead a huge, noisy country. what do you do?
o: learn to shout to be heard.
keep your own quiet, careful way, and serve.
refuse, because you're not a speechmaker.
games.why: Dr. Singh kept his quiet, careful style, close to Ang 470's sweetness and humility.

practice: Think back over a week of errands and appointments, the post office, a school office, the clinic, the road crew, and find one person who did their part well and quietly, never asking to be seen.
Hold them in mind for a few breaths; you don't need to know their name. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, with them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Nimrata. Humility, the quiet, careful style Dr. Singh showed as India's soft-spoken, turbaned prime minister. Today's word.

orig.note: nimrata, humility, a virtue Sikh teaching holds up again and again.

carryVoice: Your line: quiet service. Sweetness and humility fit at any desk, anywhere. See you tomorrow.
